fatal_errors: The proposed Mo addition and aging treatment do not reconstruct the target intervention, which is laser-assisted machining of DED-fabricated Ti33Nb28Cr11V11Ni17 using localized preheating.
No explicit Ti- and Ni-primary alloy composition is given, and the source of the proposed 5 at% Mo through elemental substitution is unspecified.
The cited evidence supports Ni- or Co-induced sigma precipitation in Al0.8NbTiV, not Mo-induced precipitation in a Ti- and Ni-primary alloy.
Testing at 1200–1600 °C is outside the target's experimentally investigated 22–1000 °C range and may dissolve or coarsen precipitates created by aging at 1050 °C.
The intervention bundles composition modification and heat treatment, so the proposed experiment cannot determine whether any effect arises from Mo, aging, or their interaction.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses high-temperature strength in a broad HEA context and offers a measurable control comparison, microscopy, mechanical testing, and a numerical falsification threshold. However, it is scientifically disconnected from the hidden study. The target concerns localized laser preheating during machining of a specified DED Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni alloy; its mechanism is transient thermal softening above roughly 800 °C, reduced cutting resistance and vibration, and mitigation of machining-induced work hardening. Its outcomes are lower cutting force, better surface roughness, less grain refinement, and no compositional change. The generated hypothesis instead predicts precipitation strengthening after Mo alloying and aging. Its central assumptions—Mo-generated fine precipitates, their stability at 1200–1600 °C, and a 10–20% strength or creep benefit—are not established by the cited evidence. The experiment is partly discriminating but needs a specified base composition, substitution rule, Mo-only and aging-only factorial controls, and phase-stability evidence at the test temperature.
